summary:
We developed Deep Space Live Monitor, an offline web dashboard that shows Earth and an astronaut’s spacecraft side by side. It simulates a mission to the ISS, the Moon or Mars. It tracks crew vitals (heart rate, sleep, SpO2, temperature), daily and cumulative radiation split into neutron and total dose, and the Earth-to-spacecraft communication link. A space view shows the spacecraft’s position and the signal beam turning strong, weak or lost.

It addresses the NASA and CSA problem that long missions combine radiation, isolation, distance and microgravity, while Earth cannot respond quickly. The spacecraft analyses health data on board and raises alerts without Earth. When the link drops, data is stored and sent when the link returns. Every score, alert and signal state explains its cause, and a statistical check flags readings that are unusual for that astronaut.

It matters because crews on Moon and Mars missions must depend on autonomous, explainable health monitoring. All data is simulated and the thresholds are illustrative. The design is ready for real wearable and radiation sensors.
details:
What it does and how it works

Deep Space Live Monitor is an offline web dashboard that simulates a crewed mission to the ISS, the Moon or Mars. It shows Earth (Ground Control) and the spacecraft side by side on one page. A simulation generates daily vitals (resting heart rate, sleep, SpO2, temperature, exercise) and radiation dose, split into neutron and total. On the spacecraft side, rule-based logic and a risk engine score sleep, cardiovascular, radiation, bone and fitness, and behavioral risk. Alerts fire without Earth, and an AI check flags readings that are unusual compared with the astronaut’s own last 14 days. A space view and a signal simulation show the link turning strong, weak or lost. While the link is lost, data packets are stored on board, then sent to Earth when it returns, with delay and late-data flags.

Benefits

  • Works with no internet, so it fits missions where help is far away.
  • Every score, alert and signal state shows its cause, the rule, the value and the action.
  • Radiation is visible against a reference limit, with a live caption.
  • Earth sees how stale its data is, which a mission team needs.

Intended impact

To show how autonomous, explainable health monitoring could support Moon and Mars crews. The same ideas could also help remote care on Earth.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with Canvas for animation and SVG for charts. No external libraries.
  • Built with AI assistance (Claude), tested headlessly with Node.js and jsdom.
  • Demo deck made with pptxgenjs.
  • Background: NASA Human Research Program pages and Canadian Space Agency articles.
  • Hardware: none yet. The planned next step is ESP32 with a MAX30102 sensor.

Creativity

The project connects the health risks, the radiation and the communication delay into one live story. The Earth view is deliberately delayed, so the demo shows the real problem. Fault buttons (solar particle event, sleep loss, treadmill failure, antenna block) let a viewer cause a problem and watch the system explain it.

Factors we considered

  • Delay and blackout: the crew must keep working with no link.
  • Explainability: no unexplained number.
  • Honesty: all data is simulated, thresholds and the 600 mSv limit are illustrative, the Mars delay is scaled down, and the AI check is a statistical z-score, not a trained model.
  • Accessibility: colour is always paired with text.
  • Scope: one crew member, no real security or login.
